reference.source: Primer on the Metabolic Bone Diseases and Disorders of Mineral Metabolism (ASBMR)
clinicalPearls: An autosomal dominant sclerosing bone dysplasia caused by activating mutations in TGFB1
Presents in childhood or adolescence with limb pain, a waddling gait, muscle weakness and wasting, and easy fatigability
Radiographs show symmetrical fusiform cortical thickening of the diaphyses of the long bones, sparing the epiphyses and metaphyses
The skull base may thicken and narrow foramina, occasionally producing cranial neuropathies, headache, and hearing or visual disturbance
The proximal myopathy and slender body habitus with reduced muscle bulk can dominate the clinical picture and mimic a primary muscle disorder
Bone turnover markers may be raised, and disease activity can wax and wane over time
Management is symptomatic; glucocorticoids can relieve bone pain and improve strength in many patients, and physical rehabilitation is important
reference.pathophysiology: Camurati-Engelmann disease results from gain-of-function mutations in the gene encoding transforming growth factor beta 1 (TGFB1). The mutations increase TGF-beta signalling, which enhances osteoblast activity and bone formation at the periosteal and endosteal surfaces of the diaphyses. The excessive but disorganised cortical apposition produces symmetrical diaphyseal hyperostosis with narrowing of the medullary canal. Involvement of the skull base can encroach on cranial nerve foramina, and altered marrow space and cytokine signalling may contribute to the anaemia and systemic features seen in some patients.
additionalDifferentials: Other craniotubular hyperostoses such as sclerosteosis and Van Buchem disease
Ribbing disease (a related but more localised diaphyseal sclerosis)
Primary inflammatory myopathy given the muscle weakness
additionalInvestigations: Plain radiographs demonstrating symmetrical fusiform diaphyseal cortical thickening
Skeletal survey or bone scintigraphy to assess extent and activity
Bone turnover markers and inflammatory markers
Cranial imaging when skull-base involvement or cranial neuropathy is suspected
Assessment of muscle strength and, where needed, tests to exclude primary myopathy
redFlags: Progressive cranial neuropathy with visual loss, deafness, or facial weakness from skull-base narrowing
Features of raised intracranial pressure or hydrocephalus
Severe intractable bone pain limiting mobility
Rapidly worsening weakness suggesting an alternative or additional diagnosis
reference.prognosis: The course is variable and often chronic; many patients have significant bone pain and weakness but a normal lifespan, and symptoms may improve in adulthood or with glucocorticoid therapy, though skull-base disease can cause lasting neurological deficits.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the proximal myopathy as a primary muscle disease and overlooking the bone dysplasia
Attributing headaches and hearing loss to unrelated causes rather than skull-base hyperostosis
Failing to recognise the symmetrical diaphyseal pattern that distinguishes it from focal lesions
Not offering a trial of glucocorticoids for disabling bone pain when appropriate
